Ada County by the numbers

Where is Ada County, Idaho, and how is it laid out?

Ada County sits in southwest Idaho and holds Boise, the state capital and county seat. Wikipedia reports a total area of 1,060 square miles, of which 1,053 is land, with the Boise River running through the northern part and the Snake River forming the southwestern edge.

The Idaho Territory legislature created the county on December 22, 1864, splitting it from Boise County. It is named for Ada Riggs, the daughter of a legislator who helped found Boise. Canyon County was later carved out of its western side in 1891.

Six cities sit inside the county: Boise, Eagle, Garden City, Kuna, Meridian and Star. Hidden Springs and Avimor are census-designated places. Four public school districts serve residents: Boise, Kuna Joint, Melba Joint and West Ada (Meridian Joint School District 2). Homeowners also pay into the College of Western Idaho taxing zone. For a seller, the district and city a house falls in decide which levies appear on the bill.

Interstate 84 and Interstate 184 carry most through traffic, along with US 20, 26 and 30 and several state highways. County roads and highways are maintained by the Ada County Highway District, a separate body from the county government.

What does the Ada County economy look like?

Ada County's job base is anchored by health care, semiconductors, higher education and public schools. The Idaho Department of Labor puts the 2025 county population at 546,141 and the 2024 median household income at $91,502, with a May 2026 unemployment rate of 3.4%.

The state's 2024 list of top employers in the county shows the mix:

EmployerTypeEmployment range (2024)
St. Luke's Regional Medical CenterPrivate10,000 or more
Micron TechnologyPrivate5,000 to 9,999
Boise State UniversityState government5,000 to 9,999
West Ada School DistrictLocal government2,500 to 4,999
St. Alphonsus Health SystemPrivate2,500 to 4,999
Boise School DistrictLocal government2,500 to 4,999
AlbertsonsPrivate2,500 to 4,999

Source: Idaho Department of Labor, Ada County profile. Only employers that agreed to release their ranges are listed.

The same profile counts 200,745 people who lived and worked in Ada County in 2023, 93,992 who commuted in from elsewhere and 46,767 who lived here and worked in other counties. Boise and Meridian supply the most workers, with Nampa and Caldwell in Canyon County next.

How does the Ada County Assessor value a house?

The Assessor must place a current market value on every taxable property each year, and Idaho law ties that value to the market as of January 1. Ada County says the appraisal looks at construction costs and recent sales, and may involve a visit to the property.

Notices for the primary assessment roll go out no later than the first Monday of June. Property that missed the primary roll is assessed on the subsequent roll, with notices no later than the fourth Monday in November. Anything still unassessed is picked up by the first Monday in January of the following year.

You can pull your notice from the Assessor's online property records. If you plan to sell, read it closely before you list or accept an offer. Wrong square footage, a missing bathroom or a garage that is really a carport are errors the office can correct, and a correct record makes the property easier to price. For official forms and contacts, start at the Ada County Assessor's appeals page.

How do you appeal an Ada County assessment?

File the appeal form with the Ada County Commissioner's Office on or before the fourth Monday of June at 5:00 p.m. The Commissioners sit as the Board of Equalization, and the office schedules your hearing.

  • Forms are online or at the Assessor's Office, 190 East Front Street, Suite 107, or at the Commissioner's Office, 200 W. Front Street, 3rd Floor, Boise.
  • The appeal addresses market value only. The county says it is not a forum to protest the amount of tax.
  • Bring five copies of your documentation: the original, one for each Commissioner and one for the Assessor.
  • List a contact person on the form so the county can reach you or your representative.

Before filing, the county encourages owners to talk with the deputy assessor who handled the property and to submit market information such as a Realtor's comparative market analysis, an independent appraisal or repair estimates. Values are sometimes adjusted at that stage.

The standard is demanding. The county quotes the rule that the assessor's value is presumed correct and that the taxpayer must show by clear and convincing evidence that relief is warranted. In practice that means sales data from the market, not opinion. The deadline falls in June, so a house that changes hands in spring should have the appeal question settled in the sale agreement.

When are Ada County property taxes due?

The first installment, or the full year, is due December 20. The second installment is due June 20 of the following year. The treasurer notes that the first installment of 2026 taxes is due by December 21, 2026, because December 20 falls on a Sunday.

DateWhat happens
January 1Market value is set; first day to apply for the homeowner's exemption or Circuit Breaker
First Monday in JuneAssessment notices mailed
June 20Last day to pay the prior year's second half without late charge
Fourth Monday in JuneLast day to file an assessment appeal
Fourth Monday in NovemberPrimary roll tax bills mailed
December 20Full-year payment or first half due

Source: Ada County Treasurer, important tax dates.

Miss a deadline and a 2% late charge is added, plus interest at 1% per month starting January 1 after the due date. When the 20th falls on a weekend or holiday, a payment postmarked on or before the 20th is timely the next business day. Delinquent notices for unpaid first-half taxes go out in January, and notices for unpaid second-half taxes go out in July.

What happens to the tax bill when an Ada County house changes hands?

Ada County bills an ownership change through a separate "missed" roll mailed in February, covering the assessment from the date of the change to December 31. That bill can surprise a buyer or seller who assumed the regular December bill covered everything.

New or finished improvements are handled on the subsequent, or occupancy, roll. Those bills are typically mailed in January and are due in June. A seller who finished an addition or a new build late in the year should expect one.

Ask the title company to pull the current balance and to check for any missed-roll or subsequent-roll bill before closing day. The Treasurer's Office answers questions at 208-287-6800 and posts bills and payment history on its online payment site. You can also reach the Treasurer through the Ada County Treasurer's Office page.

Which exemptions matter when you sell an Ada County home?

The main one is the homeowner's exemption, which cuts the taxable value of an owner-occupied primary home and up to one acre of land by 50%, to a maximum set by the state. The Idaho State Tax Commission lists the maximum as $125,000 for 2021 through 2025, and says it lasts until ownership changes or the home stops being your primary residence. A buyer therefore generally has to apply again.

  • Homeowner's exemption: applied for through the county Assessor.
  • Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker): income-based, applied for through the Assessor.
  • Reduction for 100% disabled veterans: also an Assessor application.

The state tax commission's homeowner's exemption page explains the calculation with an example. Confirm the current-year maximum with the Assessor, because we could not verify the 2026 figure.

What do Ada County sellers with back taxes usually face?

Sellers who owe back property tax in Ada County face a growing balance, because the 1% monthly interest runs on both the tax and the late charge from January 1. Inherited homes, rentals and houses with deferred repairs often reach this point when no one is watching the mail.

A cash sale can shorten the path from a delinquent notice to a payoff, since there is no lender underwriting to wait on. We buy the house as is, so repairs do not need to happen first. Any unpaid tax is settled through escrow, and the title company will give you an exact figure.

Call or text us for a written offer on an Ada County house. If the offer does not suit you, you owe us nothing.

More questions about Ada County, ID Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Ada County property tax?

Pay through the Ada County Treasurer, either online on the county's payment site or by mail. Bills and payment history are available online, and the office can be reached at 208-287-6800.

What is the Ada County property tax appeal deadline?

The deadline is 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday of June, filed with the Commissioner's Office. The appeal covers value only, not the tax amount.

Is the 2026 first installment due on December 20?

No. The Ada County Treasurer states that the first installment of 2026 taxes is due by December 21, 2026, since December 20 is a Sunday.

Does the homeowner's exemption move to the buyer?

No. The state says the exemption lasts until ownership changes or the home stops being your primary residence, so the new owner applies on their own.

Can I sell an Ada County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The balance, including the 2% late charge and monthly interest, is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the title company for a payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Kootenai County by the numbers

Where is Kootenai County and how is it laid out?

Kootenai County sits in the Idaho Panhandle, with Coeur d'Alene as both the county seat and the largest city. It covers 1,316 square miles, of which 1,244 are land and 71 are water, about 5.4 percent (Wikipedia, citing the Census Bureau). The water includes Lake Coeur d'Alene and the southernmost part of Lake Pend Oreille.

Bonner County lies to the north, Shoshone County to the east, Benewah County to the south and Spokane County, Washington, to the west. Parts of the Coeur d'Alene National Forest and the Kaniksu National Forest fall inside the county.

The incorporated cities are Athol, Coeur d'Alene, Dalton Gardens, Fernan Lake Village, Harrison, Hauser, Hayden, Hayden Lake, Huetter, Post Falls, Rathdrum, Spirit Lake, Stateline and Worley. Census-designated places include Conkling Park and Rockford Bay, and unincorporated communities include Bayview, Cataldo, Clarksville, Garwood, Lane and Medimont. A seller's address can sit in a city, on a lake or on rural land, and the rules that apply differ for each.

How did Kootenai County get started?

The Idaho Territorial Legislature created Kootenai County on December 22, 1864, and named it for the Kootenai tribe. A county government was not organized right away because there was little settlement, and the 1864 territorial census counted 81 residents.

The Mullan Road was built through the area in 1859, with a route on the north side of Lake Coeur d'Alene beginning in 1861. Rathdrum was the first of today's incorporated cities to see settlement, starting in 1861, and it became a stagecoach stop and later the county seat. Post Falls was settled in 1871. The Mission of the Sacred Heart at Cataldo finished its mission church by 1855, and that building is described as Idaho's oldest structure.

The older housing near the lake and downtown, and the newer subdivisions spreading toward Post Falls and Rathdrum, come from different eras. Sellers with an older house should expect a buyer's inspection to look closely at roof, wiring and foundation.

How fast has Kootenai County grown?

The county has roughly tripled in size since 1980. The table lists census counts and the Wikipedia 2025 estimate.

YearPopulation
198059,770
199069,795
2000108,685
2010138,494
2020171,362
2025 (estimate)191,864

Growth between 2000 and 2020 ran at 55.7 percent in the first decade and 23.7 percent in the second. That kind of change affects sellers because more neighborhoods have new construction beside older homes, and because county services and tax districts keep adjusting to a larger base.

What drives the Kootenai County economy?

Health care, schools, hospitality and retail lead the employer list. Idaho Labor Market Information lists the 2024 top employers as Kootenai Health (2,500 to 4,999 employees), then Coeur d'Alene School District, Walmart and Hagadone Hospitality (each 1,000 to 2,499), followed by Silverwood, Kootenai County, Post Falls School District, the Coeur d'Alene Tribe, Lakeland School District and North Idaho College (each 500 to 999) (Kootenai County profile).

Average 2024 employment by industry shows how the work is spread:

  • Education and health services: 17,463
  • Trade, transportation and utilities: 13,560
  • Leisure and hospitality: 11,869
  • Construction: 6,953
  • Professional and business services: 6,710
  • Manufacturing: 5,121

The same profile reports 51,599 workers who lived and worked in the county in 2023 and a county unemployment rate of 4.2 percent in December 2025. Many residents also work across the state line. The profile counts 5,031 jobs held by county residents in Spokane, Washington, 6.5 percent of the total, and 4,008 in Spokane Valley. Coeur d'Alene is 33 miles from Spokane (Idaho Labor Market Information).

What roads, schools and services do Kootenai County sellers point to?

Interstate 90 crosses the county, along with U.S. 95 and state highways 3, 41, 53, 54, 58 and 97. Citylink and Jefferson Lines provide transit service.

Six school districts serve parts of the county:

  • Coeur d'Alene School District 271
  • Kellogg Joint School District 391
  • Kootenai Joint School District 274
  • Lakeland Joint School District 272
  • Plummer-Worley Joint School District 44
  • Post Falls School District 273

North Idaho College draws on the county as its community college taxing district.

What should a Kootenai County seller know about snow, roofs and building rules?

Kootenai County uses its own snow load map and its own amendments to the building code, so a roof is judged against a local standard. The county's residential permit guide lists a minimum frost burial depth for footings of 24 inches and refers builders to the county snow load map. The guide says the county adopted its current construction codes by Ordinance 608, effective January 1, 2020 (Kootenai County permit guide).

For manufactured and mobile homes, the county code allows a legally set home that meets all county and state rules to be relocated without extra proof if it can be verified as built for a roof snow load of at least 30 pounds per square foot (Kootenai County Code, Title 7). If you are selling a manufactured home, gather the data plate and any permits before listing.

Unpermitted work is a common snag in any sale. If you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shop, ask the county building office what permits are on file. A buyer's inspector will ask the same thing.

When are Kootenai County property taxes billed, and what happens if they are late?

Kootenai County mails all tax notices annually by the fourth Monday of November, and taxes are payable on or before December 20 (Treasurer). Failure to receive a bill does not excuse payment, under Idaho Code 63-902(9).

Payment options listed by the treasurer include mail, in person, online by credit card at kcgov.us and phone at 208-446-1005, option 3. Mailed payments count as on time only with a USPS postmark on or before the due date, and the payer covers any transaction fees. Interest on delinquent tax is calculated at one percent per month starting January 1.

The treasurer's FAQ also explains the tax deed track. When real property taxes are three years delinquent, the tax collector sends a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter to the recorded owner. The owner must pay the third year in full to stop the process, and partial payments are applied but do not stop it. An owner who cannot pay may apply to the Board of County Commissioners for hardship relief at 208-446-1600 (Treasurer FAQ). The county also holds a tax deed auction for parcels that reach that stage.

How do you appeal a Kootenai County assessment?

The deadline to appeal is the fourth Monday in June, and the county says the only way to file is through the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600 (Assessor appeal page). The Board of Equalization hearing runs like a court and acts in a quasi-judicial capacity (County guide).

Bring evidence that shows the assessed value is wrong, such as a recent appraisal, repair estimates or documentation of damage. Appeals do not pause payment, so plan around the December 20 due date.

The assessor and the treasurer split the work. The assessor handles value and appeals. The treasurer handles bills, payments and delinquencies. A seller who calls the wrong office will lose time.

What does recording a deed cost in Kootenai County?

Kootenai County's recorder charges $10 for the first page and $3 for each additional page for standard documents, $5.00 per page for surveys, $11.00 for plats, and $1.00 per page for copies of recorded documents (Kootenai County Recorder). State law sets a $15.00 fee for deeds of 30 pages or less. The recorder's office hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding holidays.

When an heir, divorcing spouse or co-owner is involved, record the deed before the sale rather than during closing, so the title company has the full chain in hand.

More questions about Kootenai County, ID Property Tax Guide

What is the county seat of Kootenai County?

Coeur d'Alene is the county seat and the largest city in Kootenai County.

When are Kootenai County property tax bills mailed?

The county mails notices annually by the fourth Monday of November, and the tax is payable on or before December 20.

How do I appeal my Kootenai County property assessment?

Contact the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600 by the fourth Monday in June. The hearing before the Board of Equalization works like a court proceeding.

What happens after three years of unpaid property tax in Kootenai County?

The tax collector sends a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter to the recorded owner. Paying the third year in full stops the process, and partial payments do not.

Can I sell a Kootenai County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Ask the treasurer at 208-446-1005 for the exact payoff total, then have the title or escrow company pay it from sale proceeds. The county warns that escrow may not pay the treasurer if closing happens before annual tax information is available.

What we confirmed on official pages

Selling in Canyon County?
We buy Canyon County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Canyon County by the numbers

What is Canyon County, Idaho, like for a homeowner?

Canyon County is part of the Boise metropolitan area, west of Ada County, with Caldwell as the county seat and Nampa as its largest city. Wikipedia gives the area as 604 square miles, about 587 of them land, and lists Ada, Payette, Gem and Owyhee counties and Malheur County, Oregon, as neighbors.

The Idaho Legislature created the county from Ada County in an act approved March 7, 1891. It once held all of what became Payette County and part of Gem County. Middleton was the first European settlement, from 1863, and the railroad's arrival at Caldwell led to a town there by August 1883. Nampa was platted in 1886.

Nine cities are in the county, one of them only in part:

  • Caldwell, Nampa, Middleton and Parma
  • Greenleaf, Melba, Notus and Wilder
  • Star, mostly in Ada County

Roads are Interstate 84, US 20, 26, 30 and 95, and state highways 19, 44, 45 and 55. Part of the Deer Flat National Wildlife Refuge lies inside the county. The levy table later on this page shows that a city levy is one component of the bill, so the taxing districts listed on your notice matter.

How does the Canyon County economy affect home sellers?

The county's 2025 covered employment of 89,966 is led by trade, transportation and utilities (21,409), education and health services (19,006), construction (11,968) and manufacturing (10,869). The Idaho Department of Labor counts a 2025 population of 275,123, a 2024 median household income of $76,488 and a June 2026 unemployment rate of 3.7%.

Employer (2025)TypeEmployment range
WalmartPrivate1,000 to 2,499
Nampa School DistrictLocal government1,000 to 2,499
Vallivue School DistrictLocal government1,000 to 2,499
Saint Alphonsus Health SystemPrivate1,000 to 2,499
College of Western IdahoLocal government1,000 to 2,499
J.R. SimplotPrivate500 to 999
Amalgamated Sugar CompanyPrivate500 to 999

Source: Idaho Department of Labor, Canyon County profile. Only employers that allowed release of their ranges are listed.

Commuting is a defining feature. In 2023 an estimated 49,391 workers lived and worked in Canyon County, 38,578 came in from other counties and 65,317 residents left the county for work. Boise was the most common workplace for residents, at 29,863 jobs, ahead of Nampa at 27,427.

Who handles property tax in Canyon County?

Two elected offices split the work: the Assessor values the property and the Treasurer bills and collects. Canyon County's Assessor office says plainly that the Treasurer sends tax bills, receives payments and distributes the money to taxing districts.

  • Assessor: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 250, Caldwell; 208-454-7431; 2cAsr@canyoncounty.id.gov.
  • Treasurer: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 240, Caldwell; 208-454-7354; treas@canyoncounty.id.gov.
  • Board of Equalization: the County Commissioners, who must finish their business and adjourn by the second Monday in July.

Under Idaho Code 63-205, the assessed value must match actual market value as of January 1. The county reappraises every property on a five-year cycle and trends values in the years between. Its published guidance stresses that taxes are budget driven, not assessment driven, and that local budgets face a 3% cap plus new construction value. A single home can therefore see its bill rise even when its own value is flat.

How is a Canyon County tax bill calculated?

The bill is taxable value times the combined levy rate of every district that serves the property. The Assessor's site gives a worked example, using a sample code area.

Levy in sample code areaRate
County0.003113130
School0.005137568
City0.005811937
Special districts0.001004090
Total0.014062635

In that example a $250,000 property less a $125,000 homeowner's exemption leaves $125,000 taxable, and $125,000 times 0.014062635 comes to $1,757.83. This is an illustration from the county, not a rate for your address. Levy rates are certified by the state by the end of October, and the Treasurer posts the current list.

Your own figures are on the notice. The Assessor's assessment information page explains each line.

What is the Canyon County appeal process?

An appeal starts with an informal review and, if that fails, goes to the Board of Equalization by the fourth Monday in June. Idaho allows appeals of assessments only, not of taxes.

  • Grounds one: the property record is wrong, such as one bath instead of two, a carport recorded as a garage or 1,600 square feet recorded as 2,000.
  • Grounds two: the market value is too high, shown by similar properties that sold for less before January 1 of the current year.
  • Informal review: a meeting, call or email with the deputy assessor assigned to your area. A corrected notice usually follows within two to three weeks.
  • Formal appeal: a written form obtained from the person who conducted the review, filed under Idaho Code 63-501A.

Only arm's-length sales that closed before January 1 count, and sales after that date are not admissible. If you lose, further appeals go to the Idaho Board of Tax Appeals and then district court under Idaho Code 63-511. A hardship exemption application for the current year is also due June 20 and goes to the Board of Equalization.

When are Canyon County property taxes due, and what are the penalties?

Notices are mailed by the fourth Monday in November. The first half is due December 20 and the second half June 20 of the next year. The Treasurer says unpaid amounts accrue penalty and interest of 12% annually starting January 1.

The county also describes a 2% late charge on a first half not paid by December 20, with interest of 1% per month from January 1 on the tax and the charge. A returned check costs $20, and the county reports no formal monthly payment plan.

Two cases differ. Personal property and manufactured housing become fully delinquent if the first half is unpaid on December 20, and the entire tax is due. New construction produces a second, supplemental notice, mailed in March or April, with the full amount due June 20, prorated from the date of occupancy or completion to December 31 of the prior year.

The Treasurer adds that not receiving a tax notice does not excuse the tax, late charge or interest, citing Idaho Code 63-902(9). Anyone who bought property during the year and did not get a bill should call the office.

Which Canyon County programs reduce a bill?

Three programs, all run through the Assessor, can lower the bill. The homeowner's exemption halves the taxable value of an owner-occupied home and up to an acre of land, to a maximum the state lists as $125,000 for 2021 through 2025.

  • Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker): income based, applications January 1 through April 15.
  • Veterans Property Tax Benefit: for 100% service-connected disabled veterans, up to $1,500 off the bill on a primary residence and up to an acre; same January 1 to April 15 window.
  • Homeowner Tax Relief credit: applied to properties with a homeowner's exemption in effect before the second Monday in July.

The county notes that relief programs have shifted year to year, and that an Additional Tax Relief credit available in 2023 was not offered for 2024. Check the Treasurer's page for the current year before relying on a figure. See also the state's homeowner's exemption page.

What do Canyon County sellers dealing with a tax problem usually face?

The common problems are a missed December deadline, an inherited house nobody is paying on, and a supplemental new-construction bill that arrives after a sale is already planned. Interest at 12% a year makes a late first half grow quickly.

We buy houses as is in Canyon County, so a seller with a delinquent balance does not have to repair or clean the house before an offer. Any unpaid tax is settled through escrow at closing, and the title company can give an exact payoff.

Call or text for a written cash offer on a Canyon County house. If you decline it, you owe us nothing.

More questions about Canyon County, ID Property Tax Guide

When is the Canyon County appeal deadline?

The deadline to appeal assessed values on the regular roll is the fourth Monday in June, under Idaho Code 63-501A. Begin with an informal review before that date.

What is the Canyon County late fee for property tax?

A 2% late charge is added to an unpaid first half, and interest runs at 1% per month from January 1, which the county also describes as 12% annually.

Can I pay Canyon County property tax in installments?

Yes, in two halves: December 20 and June 20. The county says there is no formal monthly payment plan.

Can I appeal because my taxes are too high?

No. Idaho allows appeals of the assessed value only. Complaints about budgets go to the elected officials who set them.

Do I need to pay Canyon County taxes if I never got a notice?

Yes. The Treasurer cites Idaho Code 63-902(9): not receiving a notice does not excuse the tax, late charge or interest.
